## My Thinking

I have been farming this same land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father farmed it before me. I know what this ground does and what it needs.

This land is flat North China Plain soil — good loam, but the water table has been dropping. We don't get much rain here, maybe 500 mm a year if we're lucky, and most of it falls in summer when the maize doesn't need our help. For wheat, I have to pump.

I grow winter wheat and summer maize. I have always done this. My neighbors do this. The purchasing station in town buys both. I know the prices, I know the buyers, I know the timing. At my age I am not going to try cotton or vegetables on a large scale — my back gives me trouble now, and those crops need constant watching and hand work. My wife helps during planting and harvest, and my son comes back for a few days in June.

I have about 8 mu. Same field does wheat then maize — I plant wheat in early October after the land cools, harvest it in early June, then immediately plant maize in the stubble. No point letting the ground sit idle.

**Wheat:** I use the improved Jimai variety the village station recommended three years ago. It does well. For fertilizer, I put down base fertilizer before planting — diammonium phosphate mixed with urea — and then top-dress with urea at jointing. I irrigate four times: the winter water before freezing, the jointing water, the heading water, and the grain-filling water. I spray herbicide once in spring and fungicide once when the weather turns humid before heading.

**Maize:** I buy hybrid seed from the county supply cooperative —郑单958 or similar, whatever they have in stock that year. After wheat harvest I use the rotary tiller to chop the stalks and then direct-seed the maize without deep ploughing. Saves fuel, saves my knees. I water it once before tasseling if the sky doesn't cooperate, sometimes a second time if August is dry. One spray for corn borer in July.

I will not change what I'm doing this year. The plan works. I know it.
